institutional.label: St. Luke's mission hospital closes
institutional.note: The Church Missionary Society hospital on Mountain Road shuts. Its premises are the ones the Government later rents.

institutional.label: The register opens
institutional.note: The first surviving admission is entered in Notebook 1.

institutional.label: The Government takes the building
institutional.note: The rented Mountain Road premises pass into direct Government use.

institutional.label: Enlargement deferred
institutional.note: Haaretz reports that because the enlargement was deferred, "the position there became difficult in the intestinal-disease season."

institutional.label: A new hospital announced, 260 beds
institutional.note: Doar HaYom, citing al-Muqattam: 180 surgical beds and 80 for other diseases, work to begin shortly and take two years.

institutional.label: Contracted to Solel Boneh, ~£90,000
institutional.note: With a clause requiring 50 per cent Jewish and 50 per cent Arab labour.

institutional.label: Ground broken at Bat Galim
institutional.note: Some 80 Jewish and Arab workers clearing and excavating.

institutional.label: The Arab workers on the site strike
institutional.note: Their daily wage 27-32 grush against 60-75 for the Jewish carpenters; the Deputy District Commissioner promises to equalise them.

institutional.label: Standing complete on the plain
institutional.note: "The Government Hospital at Bat Galim stands sheer, complete in architectural severity."

institutional.label: Construction completed
institutional.note: Mendelsohn's assistant Dr Kampinsky, at the ceremony, dates completion to September.

institutional.label: The wards are occupied — NB20 to NB21
institutional.note: Some 150 patients transferred from Mountain Road. The register's own notebook seam falls here.

institutional.label: Opened at 225 beds
institutional.note: "I declare the hospital officially open, and I wish that it may remain empty."

institutional.label: A language incident at the opening
institutional.note: The Va'ad Leumi protests to the Chief Secretary that the speeches were not translated into Hebrew.

institutional.label: An Emergency Aid Post at the old premises
institutional.note: The Mountain Road building continues in use under its own name.

institutional.label: A death inside the gap
institutional.note: The Mitteilungsblatt records a death at the hospital in months for which no register survives.

institutional.label: A plague department is built
institutional.note: Built beside the hospital by the Public Works Department.

institutional.label: Dr Naif Amin Hamzeh honoured
institutional.note: Medical Officer at the Government Hospital, Haifa, made Hon. M.B.E.

institutional.label: The plague outbreak begins
institutional.note: 64 cases and 18 dead by November 1944.

institutional.label: An Isolation Section
institutional.note: The hospital still has an Isolation Section in 1945 — so the ward value's disappearance from the register after Feb 1940 was a clerical change, not the work leaving.

institutional.label: The Exodus deportees are landed
institutional.note: The wounded from the intercepted ship come ashore at Haifa.

institutional.label: The Jewish staff walk out
institutional.note: Reported alongside the removal of Jewish patients.

institutional.label: Jewish patients are removed
institutional.note: Corroborated by the register itself: the Jewish share of admissions falls away in the last notebook.

institutional.label: To the municipality
institutional.note: The hospital passes out of Government hands on 2 May 1948.

external.label: St. Luke's mission hospital closes
external.note: The Church Missionary Society hospital on Mountain Road shuts. Its premises are the ones the Government later rents; the register opens in them in 1930.

external.label: The 1929 riots
external.note: Communal violence from Jerusalem outward; 133 Jews and 116 Arabs killed across the country. Haifa saw far less than Hebron or Safed, but the year is the hinge on which Mandate communal policy turned.

external.label: Passfield White Paper
external.note: Restricts Jewish immigration and land purchase in the wake of the Shaw and Hope Simpson reports; effectively withdrawn by the MacDonald Letter of Feb 1931.

external.label: The Fifth Aliyah
external.note: The largest wave of the Mandate: roughly 200,000 arrivals 1932-1938, most in these four years, driven by the Nazi seizure of power. Haifa is the port of entry and its population roughly doubles in the decade.
external.source: Survey of Palestine (1946), vol. I ch. VI

external.label: The Haavara Agreement
external.note: Transfer agreement enabling German Jews to move capital to Palestine as goods; underwrites much of the Fifth Aliyah's German component.

external.label: The Jaffa demonstrations
external.note: Arab general strike and demonstrations against immigration; police fire on crowds in Jaffa and Haifa. Among the first mass casualty events of the decade in Haifa itself.

external.label: Haifa harbour opens
external.note: The deep-water port is inaugurated after five years of construction, remaking the city's labour market and its population.
external.source: Report to the Council of the League of Nations, 1933

external.label: Drought and the water crisis
external.note: A severe dry year across the country; typhoid and dysentery seasons are reported worse than usual.
external.source: Report to the Council of the League of Nations, 1934

external.label: The IPC pipeline reaches Haifa
external.note: The Iraq Petroleum Company line from Kirkuk terminates at Haifa; the refinery follows. Industrial injury enters the city's casualty pattern.
external.source: Report to the Council of the League of Nations, 1935

external.label: Izz al-Din al-Qassam killed
external.note: The Haifa-based preacher is killed by police in the hills; his funeral in Haifa becomes a mass demonstration, and his death is generally read as a trigger of the Revolt.
external.source: Survey of Palestine (1946), vol. I ch. II

external.label: The Arab Revolt
external.note: Three years of general strike, armed insurgency and British counter-insurgency. Haifa, its port and the refinery are repeatedly attacked; the Government Hospital is built through the whole of it.
external.source: Survey of Palestine (1946), vol. I ch. II

external.label: The general strike
external.note: The Revolt's first phase: a six-month Arab general strike, with Haifa port at its centre.

external.label: The Peel Commission reports partition
external.note: Recommends partitioning Palestine, with Haifa in the proposed Jewish state under temporary British mandate. Rejected by the Arab leadership; the Revolt resumes in September.

external.label: The Haifa market bombings
external.note: A series of bombings in the Arab market of Haifa, among the deadliest single incidents of the Revolt; scores killed and many more wounded, and the wounded go to the Government Hospital.

external.label: The MacDonald White Paper
external.note: Caps Jewish immigration at 75,000 over five years and restricts land transfer; the frame for the illegal-immigration years that follow.

external.label: The Second World War
external.note: Palestine becomes a rear base and, from 1940, a target. Military demand reshapes the Government Hospital's beds and staff.

external.label: Italian air raid on Haifa
external.note: Italian aircraft bomb the port and refinery area; dozens killed. The first of a series of raids on the city in 1940-1941.

external.label: The heaviest raid on Haifa
external.note: Italian bombing of the Haifa oil installations and adjacent quarters, the war's worst single day of civilian casualties in the city.

external.label: Atlit detention camp in use
external.note: Intercepted ma'apilim are held at the camp south of Haifa. Notebook 25 of this register is the camp's own admission book for 1940.

external.label: The Patria sinks in Haifa bay
external.note: The Haganah's charge intended to disable the deportation ship sinks it in the harbour; over 250 refugees and crew drown, and the survivors are landed at Haifa.

external.label: The Struma sinks
external.note: The refugee ship, refused entry to Palestine, is torpedoed after being towed from Istanbul; one survivor of some 780. A turning point in Mandate immigration politics.

external.label: Plague years in Palestine
external.note: Bubonic plague is reported in the country, with Haifa among the affected districts; the Government Hospital's plague department dates from 1942.
external.source: Annual Report of the Department of Health, 1944

external.label: Bevin announces the Anglo-American Committee
external.note: Immigration remains capped; the announcement is followed by riots in Tel Aviv and elsewhere.

external.label: Black Sabbath
external.note: Mass British arrests and searches across the country against the Jewish Agency and the Haganah.

external.label: The King David Hotel bombing
external.note: The Irgun destroys the hotel's south wing; 91 killed. Followed by curfews and searches in Haifa among other cities.

external.label: The Exodus 1947 is brought into Haifa
external.note: The intercepted immigrant ship is escorted into Haifa port; the wounded are landed and the rest deported back to Europe. The register's 1947 notebooks cover these weeks.

external.label: The UN partition resolution
external.note: Resolution 181 recommends partition; fighting begins in the country within days and does not stop.

external.label: The Haifa refinery killings
external.note: An Irgun bomb at the refinery gate is followed by the killing of Jewish refinery workers by Arab workers, and by reprisals. Among the deadliest days in the city's own war.

external.label: The battle for Haifa
external.note: Haganah operation Bi'ur Hametz takes the city over two days; the Arab population largely leaves by sea and road. The register's last notebook stops in these weeks.
external.source: Survey of Palestine and contemporary press

external.label: The Mandate ends
external.note: The British administration withdraws; the State of Israel is declared. The Government Hospital passes to the municipality on 2 May.

dav19370618-01.2.93.note: "Work has begun on the building of the Government Hospital in Bat Galim. Some 80 Jewish and Arab workers are engaged in clearing the plot and in excavation." The first naming of the site in this corpus.

dav19370905-01.2.129.note: The Arab workers on the site strike. A delegation to the Deputy District Commissioner for the North complains that their daily wage is 27–32 grush "while the wage of the Jewish carpenters comes to 60–75 grush a day." The Deputy Commissioner promises to equalise the two and to raise the latter. The 50/50 employment clause and what it was worth in practice, in one paragraph.

dav19381223-01.2.66.note: The fullest account of the ceremony. The building cost £120,000. "The plan of the hospital was drawn by the engineer Mr A. Mendelsohn." Five components: (1) a six-storey block for the beds and the nurses' quarters; (2) a three-storey block for operating theatres, outpatient reception and laboratory; (3) reception, first aid, offices and pharmacy; (4) the services wing; (5) the infectious-diseases wing. Extension is possible and there is ample room for a garden. £100,000 was allocated at first, raised to £112,000 as materials rose; 200 beds were provided for, then "24 beds were added for patients from among the military, and the budget was enlarged again." The High Commissioner's own speech says 225 beds, "befitting the needs of this city better than the old hospital building," and closes: "I declare the hospital officially open, and I wish that it may remain empty."

dav19381227-01.2.16.note: 1938-12-27, Davar, HaBoker, HaZman (dav19381227-01.2.16, hbkr19381227-01.2.17, hzh19381227-01.2.17) — The aftermath. The Va'ad Leumi writes to the Chief Secretary protesting that the speeches of the High Commissioner, the Director of Medical Services and the Mayor of Haifa "were not translated into Hebrew," which "gravely offended the feelings of the Jewish public, which sees in it a contempt for the recognised rights of the Hebrew language and for the dignity of the Yishuv." Three papers carried it; the opening was a language incident as much as a medical one.

dhy19350912-01.2.71.note: The announcement. "Al-Muqattam reports that the Government intends to build a large government hospital in Haifa. The surgical department will hold 180 beds and the department for other diseases 80. The building work will begin shortly and will take two years." A 260-bed plan, announced September 1935, promised for 1937 — and the wards were not occupied until October 1938. Read against 1933-07-03, the deferral and its answer are now both on the record.

haolam19370617-01.2.10.note: "The Government Department of Health has signed a contract with Solel Boneh for the building of the Government Hospital in Haifa. The building will cost some ninety thousand pounds; the installation work has been given to the Herut company. Among other conditions the Government stipulated that Solel Boneh employ 50 per cent Jews and 50 per cent Arabs. Work will begin in a few days."

haretz19330703-01.2.12.note: Annual review of health provision. "Because the enlargement of the Government Hospital in Haifa was deferred, the position there became difficult in the intestinal-disease season." Also: the eastern Galilee short of beds, patients falling back on the Scottish Mission hospital in Tiberias. Capacity, and a deferral that the 1935 announcement below finally answers.

haretz19381223-01.2.5.note:
The same ceremony, with two things Davar does not carry. The institution's annual budget is put at about £20,000. And Dr Kampinsky, Mendelsohn's assistant, speaking in English, "gave details of the building work and said that its construction was completed in September of this year."

September finished, October occupied, December opened. The three dates now come from three independent directions — the architect's office, the registers, and the Government's own ceremony.

haretz19441117-01.2.59.note: two new cases — a man near the former Carmel station in the west, a woman at Balad al-Sheikh by Yagur. Since 20 June: 64 cases, 18 dead, 36 recovered, 10 still in hospital

haretz19450710-01.2.24.note: A review of the Public Works Department's wartime building. Under "The war against the plague epidemic": "The Department of Public Works took part in the operations against the plague epidemic. In 1942 the Department set up a special department for plague sufferers beside the Government Hospital in Haifa, and in the same year an isolation pavilion of 14 beds was built for the government hospital at Beit Safafa near Jerusalem." Further down, among the war years' works, "to the Government Hospital in Haifa a pavilion of 20 beds was added."

haretz19480503-01.2.39.note:
the closing scene, and the terminus of the whole register.

"The Government Hospital in Haifa — to the municipality. (From our correspondent in Haifa) The Government Hospital in Haifa was transferred yesterday to the authority of the Haifa municipality and will serve from now on as a municipal hospital. This hospital contains 288 beds and is one of the largest and finest hospitals in the country. For the present there will be opened in it a department for infectious diseases, a surgical department and a clinic for the Arab population… "Our correspondent, who visited the hospital yesterday, found it completely empty. Apart from the joint guard of Jews and British policemen, a few individual British doctors and British nurses, there is not a living soul in it. He was told that immediately upon the conquest of Haifa the Arab employees and patients began to leave the hospital in masses. Many patients were transferred by ambulance to the environs of Haifa, many others were taken by boat to Acre. About 60 Arabs, the last of the patients, were taken out of the hospital last Thursday. With them went the last of the nurses, most of them Armenian. The Arab doctors also left… "Despite his personal promise, Dr Hamzi's ambulances did not return. Dr Hamzi has left for Lebanon. By contrast, praise is due to the conduct of the British chief physician, Dr MacNeil, and of the property inspector, Mr Dook (an Arab, a British subject), thanks to whom the equipment stores were preserved intact. "The interior of the hospital arouses nausea. The great halls, formerly gleaming with cleanliness, are filthy and befouled. Here and there stretchers still lie stained with blood. In the mortuary four Arab bodies were still lying last night. The beds are overturned; in the nurses' room there is no sign of order. In several departments part of the equipment is missing."

hmf19480126-01.2.34.note:
the fullest account, and it prints the findings of the special commission the Haifa Situation Committee appointed. Headline: "The Government Hospital in Haifa has become a purely Arab institution. The Jews left it because gang members took control of it."

The trigger: families of the Jewish patients demanded insistently that they be moved, and the parents of the pupils of the hospital's nursing school feared for their daughters' lives. "As a result, on 31.12.47 all the Jewish patients were transferred out of the Government Hospital, and the medical personnel left their work."

The commission's findings, which are the closest thing this corpus offers to an inspection of the wards:

- Many employees, "especially of the lower grades, appeared at the hospital armed with firearms; most also carry knives." - Threats against the nurses and trainees by low-grade employees and by "the Arab policemen stationed there to guard the prisoners." - "The wounded brought to the hospital are accompanied by their relatives and friends, or by armed gang members, and often a wounded man has armed bodyguards standing beside him day and night. These things were done openly and unhindered." - "In one case two shots were fired inside one of the hospital's lavatories." - "In one case an Arab prisoner was brought to the hospital and was spirited out of it." - "The hospital is enclosed by a stone wall about a metre and a half high," which does not answer. - "Near the turning on the Bat Galim road towards the hospital the Arab Legion is encamped. There were cases in which Arab Legion sentries threatened Jewish nurses and their escorts at gunpoint as they passed, chiefly in the evening — the threat reaching the point of loading a round into the barrel." - "Armed Arabs move about in large groups in the vicinity of the hospital and inside its courtyards, and they penetrate even into the patients' rooms. In one case several armed Arabs stopped a nurse and pointed a pistol at her; only when it became clear to them that this nurse was an Arab did they let her go."

And the settlement that failed: after weeks of negotiation "the mountain gave birth to a mouse" — two gates left open, one British and one Arab policeman at each, six more British policemen inside; no Jewish guard. The Yishuv institutions judged it insufficient.

The single most consequential sentence for this project sits in that same article, as an aside: "Incidentally: this hospital contains the only department for infectious diseases in the north of the country, and that is also the only department the Jewish population used." The Yishuv asked the Government to open an infectious-diseases department inside a Jewish settlement, offering to provide the premises if the Government supplied equipment and staff. No answer was received.

Two things follow. It sharpens `` further — for the whole north there was no separate infectious-diseases institution, this was it. And it bears on the confessional composition of the register: Jewish use of the Government Hospital was, on the Yishuv's own account, largely confined to one department.

hzh19470720-01.2.2.note:
"3 people were transferred to the Government Hospital and several sick people were taken to Atlit after being examined at the Government Hospital."

The Exodus, July 1947 (ahr19470720-01.2.11, hzh19470720-01.2.2, hmf19470721-01.2.4) — 4,389 deportees, 955 of them children; 28 sick and 34 of their relatives left in the country. "The sick sent to the Government Hospital are 17 men, 10 women and one child," with 34 relatives as escorts; 22 of them were then sent on to Atlit. Named among those who stayed: Aryeh Birenbaum (26), serious; William Milman (24), broken jaw; Ernst Weiss (24), chest wound on the left; Moshe Engelman. The dead: Zvi Yakubovitz (15), born in Bendin, Poland, of the Hancha children's kibbutz, whose brother had come before him and was in Atlit; Mordechai Baumstein (23); and a third who died in the hospital. "The dead were brought to the hospital half-naked." A woman died in childbirth — reportedly Pola Abramovitch — and her body was buried at sea. Of the wounded taken to the hospital, all were later moved to Atlit; six sick remained, "among them a girl of two ill with chickenpox, and her mother is with her."

On 21 July "three new graves were dug in the row of the martyrs of the ha'apala in the Haifa cemetery." At four in the afternoon a great crowd gathered beside the Government Hospital; the three bodies were brought out of the mortuary wrapped in blue-and-white flags and driven to the cemetery, Rabbi Dr Israel Goldstein eulogising.

Two men buried as "Abraham son of Abraham." On 11 February 1947 (dav19470212-01.2.6, hegeh19470212-01.2.8) the unknown ma'apil of the Lanegev, who died of wounds from the naval boarding, was buried from the Government Hospital in Bat Galim under that name — "the holy one who fell for the sanctification of the Name and of the Land." Nothing in his clothes identified him; his pockets held a comb in a leather case, a cigarette case and an empty notebook with a few unclear words. Minutes before the funeral a driver arrived saying he thought the dead man was his brother-in-law: Harry Laufer, born in Leipzig, a teacher of English, whose wife Barbara Seligman-Laufer had been deported to Cyprus with the rest. And in December 1946 (haretz19461206-01.2.74) the inquest on two Knesset Yisrael immigrants — Isaac Rosenbaum and an unknown "buried under the name Abraham son of Abraham" — heard "the testimony of the physician of the Government Hospital, who examined the bodies of the dead and performed autopsies on them," and found both died of army bullets, one to the head, one to the lungs and heart.

Anyone reading unnamed entries in the 1946–47 ledgers should know that this formula existed and what it covered.

mb19400308.pub: Mitteilungsblatt der Hitachdut Olej Germania we Austria
mb19400308.orig: Am Dienstag abend starb im Regierungskrankenhaus in Haifa Lipmann Lipschitz, ein 27-jähriger aus Lettland stammender Jude, an den Verletzungen, die er bei der Demonstration erlitten hatte. An dem Begräbnis am Mittwoch nahmen unabsehbare Menschenmassen teil.
mb19400308.trans: On Tuesday evening Lipmann Lipschitz, a 27-year-old Jew originally from Latvia, died in the Government Hospital in Haifa of the injuries he suffered at the demonstration. Immense crowds attended the burial on Wednesday.
mb19400308.note: Tuesday evening is 5 March 1940. Notebook 24 ends on 1 March 1940 and nothing resumes until Notebook 29 on 8 February 1944, so this death falls four days inside the register's gap and cannot be checked against it at all. That is the point of it: it establishes from outside that the hospital was admitting patients and its deaths were being reported — which means the missing notebooks are missing, not never-written. Jüdische Weltrundschau carries the same event on 11 March.
